lesson.title: remove(): Deleting by Value, Not by Position
lesson.summary: How .remove(value) searches for the first matching element and deletes it in place, why it raises an error when the value is missing, and how it differs from position-based deletion.
lesson.body:
Every method covered so far, append and insert, cares about position: where in the list something goes. remove flips that around entirely. Instead of telling Python where to delete from, you tell it what value to get rid of, and Python figures out where that value lives. This matches how people usually think about deleting things: you rarely think "remove whatever is at position 3," you think "get rid of the shield," and remove is built for exactly that request.

The syntax is list.remove(value). Python scans the list from the front and deletes the first element that equals value, shifting everything after it one position to the left to close the gap. Like append and insert, remove mutates the list in place and returns None; there is nothing to save from the call itself.

inventory = ["sword", "shield", "potion", "shield", "map"]
inventory.remove("shield")
print(inventory)

result = inventory.remove("map")
print(inventory)
print(result)

Trace this carefully, especially the duplicate values. inventory starts with two separate "shield" entries, at index 1 and index 3. inventory.remove("shield") removes only the first one it finds, the one at index 1, leaving the second "shield" untouched. The list becomes ["sword", "potion", "shield", "map"], which is what the first print shows; notice that "shield" still appears once, since remove never deletes every match, only the earliest one.

result = inventory.remove("map") removes "map" from ["sword", "potion", "shield", "map"], its only occurrence, at index 3. The list becomes ["sword", "potion", "shield"], so the second print shows that. Since remove always returns None regardless of what it deleted, result is assigned None, and the third print confirms that directly.

If the value you ask for is not in the list at all, remove does not fail quietly; it raises a ValueError, something like ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list. Calling inventory.remove("bow") on the list above would crash the program, since no "bow" exists in it. This is a common source of runtime errors, especially when removing something based on user input. The safe habit is to check membership first with an if value in my_list guard, or wrap the call in a try and except block.

It is worth contrasting remove with del and with pop, covered next. del my_list[2] deletes by position, like insert adds by position, and also returns nothing. pop, by contrast, deletes by position but hands back the value it removed, making it the tool of choice when you want to use the item you took out rather than simply discard it.

Because remove only deletes the first match, clearing every occurrence of a value takes more than one call. A common pattern is a while loop that rechecks membership before each removal.

readings = [0, 12, 0, 7, 0, 3]
while 0 in readings:
    readings.remove(0)
print(readings)

Trace it: readings starts with three zeros mixed among the real readings. 0 in readings is True, so the loop removes the first zero, at index 0, giving [12, 0, 7, 0, 3]. The condition is checked again, still True, another zero is removed, giving [12, 7, 0, 3], and then again, giving [12, 7, 3], at which point 0 in readings is finally False and the loop stops. The final print shows [12, 7, 3]. Writing for value in readings and calling remove inside that loop would be a mistake, since removing elements while a for loop iterates over the same list can skip elements as the list shrinks; the while and in combination avoids that by rechecking membership fresh on every pass.
